# Gatekeeper

> An access-control SaaS built in public, one quality gate at a time.

Gatekeeper is the running example and companion code for the book
**[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)**
by Tom Gilkison.

The book's premise: AI can write the code, but it cannot be trusted to
ship it. Gatekeeper starts life as an AI-generated app with no tests,
no CI, and no guardrails. Across the book it earns a layered system of
quality "gates" until its code is safe to merge on green, with the
human designing and verifying instead of typing.

## Follow along

Each chapter adds one gate. Every chapter's end state is a git tag, so
you can check out the code exactly as it stands at any point in the
book:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/TGilkison/Gatekeeper.git
cd Gatekeeper
git checkout chapter-06   # the code at the end of Chapter 6
```

## Tech

C# / .NET 8, ASP.NET Core Blazor Web App. Chosen for the strongest,
most cohesive quality-gate tooling of any mainstream stack: a real
compiler as the first gate, Roslyn analyzers, NetArchTest for
architecture, and Stryker.NET for mutation testing. The book explains
the why.

## License

MIT. Use it, fork it, copy the gate configs into your own projects.
That is the point: the book teaches you to build these gates; this repo
is where you can see them working and lift them.

## The book

[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)

Done. Gatekeeper's data layer, auth, and admin console are built and verified working end to end against your Postgres database.

## What's there

**Domain model** (`src/Gatekeeper.Web/Data/`)
- `Customer` — tenant with a `PlanTier` enum (Free / Pro / Enterprise)
- `ApplicationUser` — ASP.NET Identity login account, scoped to a customer
- `Role` — self-referencing `ParentRoleId` for the hierarchy; separate from Identity roles
- `Grant` — Allow/Deny of a permission on a resource, hanging off **either** a user or a role (enforced by a DB check constraint: exactly one subject)
- `UserRole` — role assignments
- `AuditLogEntry` — who/what/when for every console change
- `GatekeeperDbContext : IdentityDbContext` — relationships, enum-as-text conversions, unique indexes

**Console** (`Components/Pages/`) — Dashboard, Customers, Users, Roles, Grants, Audit log. Full create/edit/delete on customers/roles, user creation via `UserManager` + role assignment, grant creation with cascading customer→subject dropdowns, and a filterable read-only audit view. Every mutation writes an audit entry via a scoped `IAuditLogger` that captures the signed-in operator.

**Auth** — ASP.NET Core Identity (login/register/logout/manage) ported from the official template; every admin route is `[Authorize]`-gated and redirects to login. EF Core on Npgsql; the app auto-creates, migrates, and seeds on first run.

## To demo it

```bash
cd src/Gatekeeper.Web
dotnet run
```

Log in with the seeded admin: **`admin@gatekeeper.local`** / **`Admin!23456`**. It comes pre-seeded with an *Acme Inc* (Pro) tenant, a Member→Manager role hierarchy, and three sample grants.

## Things worth knowing

- **I verified the full flow in a headless browser**, not just a compile: login → create/edit/delete a customer, create a role under a parent, create a user + assign a role, create a grant — each persisted to Postgres and produced the right audit-log entry.
- **The connection string has no password** (as you gave it), which worked via local trust auth. If you demo on a machine where `postgres` needs a password, add `;Password=...` in `appsettings.json`.
- **One non-obvious fix baked in:** the interactive data pages use `@rendermode InteractiveServer` with **prerender disabled**. With prerender on, these load-data-on-init pages hydrated as dead HTML (buttons did nothing) — a known Blazor Web App pitfall. Disabling prerender makes them fully interactive; the trade-off is a brief moment before content appears, which is fine for an admin console.
- I added a local `dotnet-ef` tool manifest (`.config/`) and the initial migration (`Migrations/`). I did **not** commit anything — the working tree is staged for you to review.

One deliberate gap, per your note: there's **no permission-check/evaluation logic yet** — this is purely the data + admin side. When you're ready to wire up "can user X do Y on Z," the grant/role-inheritance model is already shaped for it.
